name: e09_significance
title: 9. Is any edge statistically real? Sharpe inference, timing tests and multiple testing
text:
**Question.** After accounting for sampling noise, the rule's trade structure and testing 12 assets at once, is there reliable evidence that EMA 50/200 beats buy-and-hold?

**Setup.** Full history per asset (median 22 years), default research settings. Paired stationary bootstrap (20-day mean blocks, 5,000 resamples) for Sharpe and drawdown differences; random-entry Monte Carlo (5,000 shuffles of the rule's own trades) for timing; Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) corrections across the 12 assets.

**Findings.**

- The rule has the higher Sharpe on 6 of 12 assets, but none is significant at 5% even before correction. The median 95% CI is 0.58 Sharpe units wide against a median absolute difference of 0.05. The largest gap (QQQ, +0.20) has p = 0.093, BH q = 0.760.
- SPY: Sharpe 0.59 vs 0.53, difference CI [-0.17, 0.33], p = 0.322 (not significant). PSR: P(SR > 0) = 0.999, but P(SR > B&H) = 0.68; MinTRL to confirm the gap is 378 years (median finite 466; infinite on the 6 assets where the rule trails).
- Timing: the rule beats the random-timing mean on 10 of 12 assets, but random entry is rejected at 5% on only 1 (QQQ p = 0.019), 0 after BH. SPY: 0.59 vs a random-timing mean of 0.46, p = 0.080.
- Lo (2002) Sharpes are a median 1.08x (rule) and 1.10x (B&H) the naive ones, higher because short-lag autocorrelation of daily returns is negative; no sign of the difference flips.
- Risk: max drawdown is shallower on 12 of 12 assets (SPY -36% vs -55%, difference CI [-9%, 31%]), significant after BH on 0 (0/0/0/1 with 20/60/125/250-day blocks). Volatility is significantly lower on 12 of 12. Against a static mix with the same average exposure, drawdowns are shallower on 9 of 12, 0 significantly.
- Start date: section 3 compares grid cells on a common window that opens after the EMA 400 warm-up (SPY 1996-09, QQQ 2002-11), later than the full-history start used here. QQQ's +0.20 rests on Jan 2001-Nov 2002 (rule +5.0% vs buy-and-hold -54.9%); from Nov 2002 the gap is +0.00. SPY's +0.06 barely depends on the start: from Sep 1996 the gap is +0.05.
- The notebook's own sample (NVDA 2022-2024, 3.0 years): Sharpe difference +0.09, CI [-0.57, 0.76], p = 0.383, MinTRL 83 years.

**Interpretation.** Even with the two return streams 0.72 correlated, the paired bootstrap leaves a standard error of about 0.15 on the Sharpe difference, so gaps of 0.1-0.2 are noise; MinTRL (Bailey & Lopez de Prado 2012) converts that into centuries. Quoting the best of 12 assets is the data-snooping trap of Sullivan, Timmermann & White (1999), and Holm/BH are the minimum haircut (Harvey & Liu 2015). Random in-and-out timing at exposure e earns about √e times B&H's Sharpe (median ratio 1.00), because the mean scales with e and volatility with √e. Beating that null is a lower bar than beating B&H, and it is cleared significantly on no asset after correction. The risk claim holds in *direction*, not per-asset significance: shallower drawdowns on 12 of 12 assets (sign-test p < 0.001 if assets were independent, which they are not) are the long-only, single-asset counterpart of Faber's (2007) moving-average timing result and of the crisis behaviour Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017) document for diversified trend following, but a max drawdown rests on one or two episodes, so single-asset tests rarely reject. Lower volatility is close to mechanical, and an exposure-matched static mix delivers a median 73% of the drawdown gap with no timing at all. The defensible claim is "similar risk-adjusted return, smaller drawdowns", not "alpha".
after: **Method notes.** p-values are one-sided (H0: the rule is no better). Holm controls the probability of any false rejection across the 12 assets under any dependence. Benjamini-Hochberg controls the expected share of false discoveries and is valid under independence or positive regression dependence (Benjamini & Yekutieli 2001). Equity tests are positively dependent, but bond and equity tests need not be. With no BH rejections in the Sharpe, timing or drawdown tests, the choice between Holm and BH does not change any conclusion here. PSR and MinTRL against B&H are paired (`sharpe_difference_test`): the variance of the Sharpe difference uses both legs' skewness and kurtosis and their correlation (median 0.72; Jobson-Korkie / Memmel 2003 covariance term), rather than treating B&H's estimated Sharpe as a known constant. Unlike the paired bootstrap they assume serially independent returns. The Sharpe p-value centres the bootstrap distribution on zero. The drawdown distribution is skewed and sits below the full-sample estimate, which is why the forest plot's drawdown points sit near the top of their CIs. The drawdown and volatility p-values are therefore percentile ones (the bootstrap share of differences on the wrong side of zero), consistent with the CIs. A centred test would be significant after BH on 10 of 12 assets (SPY p = 0.006), but lengthening the blocks from 20 to 250 days moves the median resampled gap from 11% to 16% (actual 18%) and cuts the centred test's rejections from 10 to 4, while the percentile test gives 0/0/0/1 rejections across 20/60/125/250-day blocks. The centred test's apparent significance therefore mostly reflects the resampling bias, which is why we report the percentile version. The block-length rows use 1,000 resamples. Max drawdown is a single-path extreme, effectively one or two independent episodes per asset, so treat its p-values as indicative. The exposure-matched mix holds the rule's average exposure in the asset and the rest in T-bills, rebalanced daily without costs. For SPY the unpaired bootstrap 95% intervals for max drawdown (`bootstrap_metric_ci`, 2,000 resamples) are [-53%, -19%] for the rule and [-63%, -28%] for B&H. They overlap. Comparing marginal intervals ignores the strong correlation between the two return streams, which is why the paired test is the right one. The universe is not free of hindsight: NVDA is included because the notebook picked it after its run-up, and Bitcoin is an extreme survivor. That inflates both legs, one reason to test differences rather than levels.

SPY random-entry null: Sharpe ratios of the rule's own trades placed at random times, with the actual rule, buy-and-hold and the sqrt(exposure)-diluted buy-and-hold Sharpe marked.
